note.explanation: Computational thinking starts by understanding the problem, then simplifying it into manageable parts, and choosing and planning a suitable solution.
examples: Before building a school website, find out what pages it needs, who will use it, and what tools are available.
To design a website, split the work into layout, content, and functionality.
note.checkAnswer: Break the problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems.
note.simple: First understand what needs to be done. Then divide the work into smaller parts and plan a suitable way to complete them.
note.title: Principles of Computational Thinking
steps: Understand the problem and identify its requirements.
Set clear objectives for the outcome.
Break a complex problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems.
Evaluate possible approaches and select an efficient solution.
Create a detailed plan or algorithm for the solution.
note.answer: The three principles in this section are problem understanding, problem simplification, and solution selection and design.

written.text: Imagine you are asked to build a website for your school. Before jumping into coding, you need to understand the problem:
written.finalAnswer: Identify the website's requirements, users, and available technical resources before planning or coding.

rubric.why: Identifying required features shows that the problem has been understood.
rubric.how: Mention that the required pages or features should be identified.

rubric.why: Considering users and resources helps ensure the planned website is suitable and possible to build.
rubric.how: Name the intended users and/or check the available tools and resources.

modelAnswer: Identify the required features, such as pages for news, events, class schedules, and contact information.
Identify the users, such as students, teachers, and parents, to help design a user-friendly interface.
Check the available resources and tools, such as a web server and the necessary software.
Final answer: Understand the requirements, users, and technical constraints before planning and building the website.

written.text: Q7.4. Discuss the concept of decomposition in computational thinking. Why is it important?
written.finalAnswer: Decomposition breaks a problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems, making it easier to solve and plan.

rubric.why: A correct description of decomposition is essential to answering the question.
rubric.how: Explain that it means breaking a problem into smaller parts or sub-problems.

rubric.why: The section specifically describes the parts as smaller and more manageable sub-problems.

rubric.why: Explaining why decomposition helps shows its practical importance in problem-solving.
rubric.how: Explain that smaller parts are easier to handle, solve, or plan.

rubric.why: A relevant example demonstrates how a large task can be divided into manageable tasks.
rubric.description: Give an example and state the final answer.
rubric.how: Use the website example by naming tasks such as layout, content, and functionality; conclude with the definition.

modelAnswer: Decomposition means breaking a problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems.
It is important because each smaller part is easier to understand, plan, and solve than the whole problem at once.
For example, when designing a website, the work can be divided into designing the layout, creating content, and coding the functionality.
These smaller tasks help organise the work and make the larger problem more manageable.
Final answer: Decomposition is breaking a problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems so that it is easier to plan and solve.

explain.title: Understand the problem first
explain.body: Understanding a problem involves identifying the core issue, defining the requirements, and setting the objectives. Before trying to solve a problem, find out what needs to be done and what the result should be. This helps you focus, set clear goals, choose efficient methods, and avoid mistakes.

explain.title: Simplify a problem
explain.body: Simplifying a problem involves breaking it down into smaller, more manageable sub-problems. For example, designing a website can be split into designing the layout, creating content, and coding the functionality.

explain.title: Select and design a solution
explain.body: Choosing the best solution involves evaluating different approaches and selecting the most efficient one. Designing the solution requires creating a detailed plan or algorithm.

mistakes: Starting to code before identifying the problem's requirements and objectives.
Confusing problem simplification with adding more details; simplification means splitting the problem into manageable sub-problems.
Choosing a solution without evaluating whether it is efficient.
Giving an example without explaining how it connects to the principle.
